opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think one of the interesting things about SWE-bench is that the tasks come from real GitHub issues in real open-source repos, so the agent is dropped into a codebase it's never seen before. That's a pretty different situation from how most people actually use coding assistants day to day. When you're working with a model in your own project, you usually already know where the relevant code lives. You might paste in the file, or point it at the function you care about, so a lot of the search problem is already solved by the human.

In SWE-bench, the model gets an issue description, which is often written by someone who has a vague idea of what's wrong, and then it has to figure out on its own where in a fairly large repository the problem actually is. So a big part of the difficulty is really localization: exploring the directory structure, grepping around, reading files, forming a hypothesis, and sometimes realizing it was wrong and backtracking. In a lot of cases, once the model finds the right spot, the actual fix is only a few lines. The hard part was getting there.

That makes it a good test of agentic behavior specifically, because the model has to be persistent and somewhat methodical. One thing we noticed is that models that were too eager would find something that looked plausible, make an edit, and declare victory. Models that did better would take the time to reproduce the bug first, write a little script to confirm the behavior, and then check that the fix actually worked. So the benchmark rewards that loop of explore, verify, and iterate more than raw code-writing ability.

I'd add one caveat, though. SWE-bench is skewed toward certain kinds of repos, mostly mature Python libraries with decent test suites and fairly conventional structure. Real-world codebases can be much messier, with weird build systems, multiple languages, internal tooling, and so on. So in some ways it understates how hard search can be in practice. But in another way it overstates the difficulty compared to general assistance, because in the real world you usually have a human in the loop who can just say "no, look over here." I think both perspectives are useful, and the benchmark is most valuable as a signal for how well a model can operate autonomously when nobody is holding its hand.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think SWE-bench is interesting because the search problem is actually pretty constrained in a way that makes it easier than a lot of real-world coding. Every SWE-bench task starts with a GitHub issue, and that issue almost always contains a stack trace, or a function name, or an error message that you can just grep for. So the agent doesn't really have to do open-ended exploration of a codebase. It has a very strong signal about where to start, and it usually only has to touch one or two files. We looked at this when we were building our SWE-bench scaffold, and honestly the most important thing was just giving the model a good bash tool and a good file editing tool and letting it grep around. We didn't need fancy retrieval, embeddings, repo maps, any of that. The model would read the issue, search for the relevant symbols, open the file, and start working.

The flip side is that this makes SWE-bench a little unrepresentative of what happens when someone's actually using Claude Code or a coding assistant in their day job. There, the task is often something like "add this feature" or "refactor how we handle authentication," and there's no stack trace pointing you at a file. The model has to build a mental model of how the codebase is organized, figure out conventions, find the three places that all need to change together, and that's a genuinely harder search problem. You also have the problem that the person asking may not know where things live either, so you can't lean on the user to give you the pointer.

So I'd say SWE-bench tests a specific slice of agentic coding really well, which is: given a well-specified bug, can you localize it and fix it without breaking the tests. And that's a real skill. But I'd be cautious about reading a SWE-bench score as a measure of how good a model is at navigating a large unfamiliar repo with a vague request. Those are different capabilities, and the second one is where I think a lot of the interesting work is right now, both on the model side and on the tooling side, like how do you give the model the right affordances to explore efficiently without blowing up the context window.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-bench issues often include a stack trace or other searchable clue, making it easier to find where to start, while general coding-assistant requests often lack a stack trace and require harder codebase exploration.

astra-6.text:
I think SWE-bench makes the search problem a little easier in one important way: you’re given a specific issue, and you know the answer is somewhere in that repository. You still have to find the relevant code, understand what’s going wrong, and figure out how to test the fix. That can take a lot of digging, but the search has a fairly clear boundary.

With general coding assistance, figuring out what to search for can itself be a big part of the task. Does the user want a change in this repository? Is there context in another service or in documentation? Is their description of the problem actually pointing at the right thing? So SWE-bench can involve very difficult coding, while still giving the agent a more constrained search problem than you encounter in everyday software engineering.

sol-6.1.text:
I think SWE-bench makes search unusually important because you’re dropping the agent into an unfamiliar repository and asking it to fix a specific issue. Before it can write the patch, it has to figure out where the relevant behavior lives, how the pieces connect, and which tests matter. The actual code change might be pretty small, but finding that change can be most of the work.

With general coding assistance, the human often supplies a lot of that context implicitly: you’ve got the relevant file open, you’ve selected a function, or you’re asking for a change in code you’re already working on. So the assistant starts much closer to the answer. SWE-bench puts more of the burden on the agent to navigate the codebase and decide what to investigate next.
